title: Obedience (ch. 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tools of good works, chapter four: a long toolbox of a list that ends on God's mercy. Your line was never despair. Which tool did you pick up? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

A teenager is asked to take the trash out. He says sure. He even does it. But all the way down the driveway there's a speech running in his head: why is it always me, nobody else ever does this, I was in the middle of something. The trash makes it to the curb. So does a small gray cloud. The job got done. Did the thing that was asked for get done? Saint Benedict, writing a rule for monks, gives that cloud a name. He calls it murmuring. And in chapter five he goes after it, because in his Rule the task is only half of the matter. Today: obedience.
screen: `SURE, AND A SPEECH IN HIS HEAD.` → `THE TRASH GOES OUT. SO DOES A CLOUD.` → `BENEDICT CALLS IT MURMURING.`

segments.voice: Chapter five opens plainly: the first step of humility is obedience without delay. Then Benedict draws a picture. A monk is told to do something, and he puts down what's in his hands and leaves it unfinished, so that the hearing and the doing happen almost together. He ties this to words of Jesus in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that heareth you, heareth me." For Benedict, a word from the abbot is answered as though God were the one asking. Then he raises the bar. Doing the thing isn't enough. It should be done without hesitating, without dragging the feet, without coldness, without grumbling, and without a reply that shows unwillingness. And he means the grumbling inside, too. If a monk obeys but murmurs in his heart, Benedict says, God sees the heart, and the work isn't accepted. For the other side he borrows a line from Paul: "God loveth a cheerful giver." That's a high bar, and the Rule keeps it human in two ways. In a later chapter, a monk handed something that seems impossible may go to his superior, patiently and at a fitting moment, and explain why. Obedience isn't pretending a heavy load is light. And near the end of the Rule, Benedict says obedience is a good to be shown not only to the abbot but to one another. So it isn't just a chain of command running downhill. It's a whole house leaning toward yes. Outside a monastery, nobody vows obedience to an abbot. But anyone can notice the speech that runs under a chore, and let it go quiet.
screen: `OBEDIENCE WITHOUT DELAY.` · `HE THAT HEARETH YOU, HEARETH ME.` · `NOT EVEN MURMURING IN THE HEART.` · `YOU MAY EXPLAIN. OBEY ONE ANOTHER.` · then, large: `GOD LOVETH A CHEERFUL GIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing without grumbling. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one task waiting for you today that you'd rather skip. The dishes, an email, a phone call. Picture yourself starting it. Listen for the speech that starts up with it, the why me, the not now. Don't argue with the speech. Just notice it, and on the out-breath, let it get quieter. Then picture doing the task with the speech switched off, hands just doing what hands do. If you pray, you can offer the task to God before you begin. The bell holds the time.
Obedience. For Benedict, a ready yes, given without delay and without grumbling, out loud or inside. Today's word.
Your line: no murmuring. Today, do one thing you'd rather not, and catch the speech before it starts. If it starts anyway, finish the job and drop the speech. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns promise obedience when they make their vows, and the community hears the Rule read aloud, including chapter five on obedience without delay or grumbling.

fork.reveal: Benedict pictures a monk leaving his work unfinished, so hearing and doing happen almost together, and doing it without grumbling.

original.note: Latin, the language of the Rule: obedience, the subject of chapter five.

trapdoor: what you thought: obedience means doing what you're told.
what it means: for Benedict, a ready yes, without delay, and without the grumbling that rides along inside.
what a scholar hears: the Rule balances it: a monk may explain an impossible task, and obedience is owed to one another, not only to the abbot.

notes: The Rule is paraphrased throughout; no English translation of the Rule is on the public-domain list. Check: ch. 5 opens 'the first degree of humility is obedience without delay'; the monk leaves his work unfinished; the list 'not timidly, not tardily, not tepidly, not with murmuring, not with a reply showing unwillingness' is paraphrased as 'without hesitating, without dragging the feet, without coldness, without grumbling'; murmuring in the heart makes the work unacceptable to God.
Ch. 68 (impossible tasks: the monk may explain to his superior patiently and at a fitting time) and ch. 71 (obedience to one another) are summarized; confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Luke 10:16 and 2 Corinthians 9:7, both quoted in RB 5.
Pronunciation of 'oboedientia' given in Church Latin style; confirm.
howItsDone: confirm that obedience is among the Benedictine vows as phrased (the vow formula of RB 58 is stability, conversatio morum, obedience).
